Daniel’s meme works because it treats “eyes” (目) as a scalar you can optimize by brute-force scaling a local pattern—one-eye small triangle, ten-eye middle triangle, hundred-eye big triangle—while quietly relying on the reader to already know the Go premise that *two* eyes is the real threshold for life. That hidden premise is exactly what makes the joke land: once “enough to live” is satisfied, the marginal value of additional eyes collapses, and the pictured construction starts to look like an almost parodic case of *overconcentration*—investing moves to make something already safe even safer, while conceding initiative and outside influence.

That tension echoes two established ideas Daniel doesn’t name. First is Go shape theory’s suspicion of the triangle as “bad shape,” especially the [empty triangle](https://senseis.xmp.net/?EmptyTriangle), because it wastes tempo for local solidity. Second is the broader measurement trap formalized as [Goodhart’s law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law): when a proxy metric (“how many eyes?”) becomes the target, it stops tracking what you actually want (efficient life, sente, influence, points). The “hundred-eye” escalation is funny precisely because it pushes the proxy to an absurd extreme and exposes how little it means beyond the constraint it was meant to satisfy.

One small blind spot is that, without even a sentence of framing, the post risks reading as pure visual gag rather than a compact critique of optimization-by-proxy. A minimal caption like “two eyes is enough” would turn it from in-joke into a more general statement about how local maximization can be strategically anti-global—on the Go board and elsewhere.
